name: Friedreich Ataxia

prevalence.range: 1 in 20,000 to 1 in 50,000 in European populations

ethnicAssociations: Most common in populations of European descent
Very rare in East Asian, Sub-Saharan African, and Native American populations

criteria.description: Absent lower limb deep tendon reflexes
Homozygous GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in FXN gene (typically 66-1700 repeats; normal <33)
Axonal sensory neuropathy on nerve conduction studies

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Progressive ataxia with areflexia and confirmatory homozygous GAA expansion in FXN gene. ~96% are homozygous for GAA expansion; ~4% are compound heterozygous (GAA expansion + point mutation).
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Late-onset Friedreich ataxia (LOFA, onset >25 years) and very late-onset (VLOFA, onset >40 years) are recognized with slower progression. GAA repeat length inversely correlates with onset age. Frataxin protein deficiency causes mitochondrial iron accumulation.

pathognomonic.notes: Combination of ataxia with absent reflexes is highly characteristic; distinguishes from other ataxias
Present in ~60-75%; major cause of morbidity and mortality

pathognomonic.symptomName: Friedreich foot (pes cavus with hammer toes)

occasional.notes: Impaired glucose tolerance in ~30%; frank diabetes in ~10-15%

rare.notes: Atrial fibrillation; can cause sudden death
Less prominent than in other cerebellar ataxias
Generally preserved cognition; mild executive dysfunction reported

laboratory: Genetic testing: homozygous GAA repeat expansion in FXN gene (diagnostic)
Fasting glucose and HbA1c for diabetes screening
imaging: MRI brain: cerebellar atrophy (mild; less prominent than other cerebellar ataxias)
MRI spine: spinal cord atrophy (cervical cord thinning)
Cardiac MRI: myocardial fibrosis, iron deposition
genetic: FXN gene (chromosome 9q21): homozygous GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion
Inverse correlation between GAA repeat length and onset age
~96% homozygous GAA expansion; ~4% compound heterozygous (GAA + point mutation)
other: Nerve conduction studies: absent or severely reduced sensory nerve action potentials (axonal sensory neuropathy)

distinguishingFeatures: SCAs usually have preserved or brisk reflexes
SCAs do not have sensory neuropathy as prominently
HSP has spasticity as predominant feature, not ataxia
HSP does not have sensory neuropathy or cardiomyopathy
AVED has low serum vitamin E levels
AVED is treatable with vitamin E supplementation
Clinically very similar to FA; must be excluded

redFlags: Cardiomyopathy is the leading cause of death - annual echocardiography mandatory
Cardiac arrhythmias can cause sudden death; ECG monitoring recommended
Omaveloxolone (Skyclarys) FDA-approved 2023 for FA age 16+; first approved therapy
Diabetes screening should be performed annually
Scoliosis may require surgical intervention if progressive
Absence of GAA expansion should prompt testing for other ataxias (SCA, AT, AVED, AOA)
references: Pandolfo M. Friedreich ataxia: the clinical picture. J Neurol. 2009;256(Suppl 1):3-8.
Cook A, Giunti P. Friedreich's ataxia: clinical features, pathogenesis and management. Br Med Bull. 2017;124(1):19-30.
Lynch DR, et al. Safety, pharmacodynamics, and potential benefit of omaveloxolone in Friedreich ataxia. Ann Clin Transl Neurol. 2019;6(1):15-26.
Delatycki MB, Bidichandani SI. Friedreich ataxia - pathogenesis and implications for therapies. Neurobiol Dis. 2019;132:104606.
